properties.headline: Fire Weather Watch issued August 13 at 12:07PM PDT until August 14 at 9:00PM PDT by NWS Pendleton OR
properties.description:
...MONSOON MOISTURE WILL BRING SCATTERED THUNDERSTORMS TODAY
THROUGH TOMORROW...

.A push of monsoon moisture will bring scattered thunderstorms to
the region this afternoon into friday evening. Lingering dry
surface air will limit the rainfall amounts today, increasing
concern for lightning ignitions. Heavier rainfall is expected
within rain cores with storms Friday, but lightning outside of
rain cores continues to be a concern.

The National Weather Service in Pendleton has issued a Fire
Weather Watch for abundant lightning, which is in effect from
Friday afternoon through Friday evening.

* AFFECTED AREA...Fire Weather Zone 695 East Washington South
Central Cascade Mountains.

* TIMING...For the Red Flag Warning, until 9 PM PDT this
evening. For the Fire Weather Watch, from Friday afternoon
through Friday evening.

* IMPACTS...Any fire that develops will catch and spread
quickly. Outdoor burning is not recommended.

* THUNDERSTORMS...Scattered coverage with abundant lightning.

* OUTFLOW WINDS...Gusty erratic winds up to 40 mph.
properties.instruction:
A Red Flag Warning means that critical fire weather conditions
are either occurring now, or will shortly. A combination of
strong winds, low relative humidity, and warm temperatures can
contribute to extreme fire behavior.

A Fire Weather Watch means that critical fire weather conditions
are forecast to occur. Listen for later forecasts and possible

from Friday afternoon through Friday evening.

Olympic Mountains, Fire Weather Zone 658 West Slopes of the
North Cascades Generally above 1500 Feet, Fire Weather Zone

Mountains.

possible across the Cascades and Olympics.

gusty and erratic outflow winds between 20 and 30 miles per
hour. Outflow winds can occur ahead of and behind storms and
cause erratic wind directions.

fire starts. Thunderstorms can also bring sudden sharp wind
shifts on existing fires, causing rapid changes in a fire's
rate of spread and direction of spread. Thunderstorm outflow
winds can be a threat for several hours following the start of
a new lightning-caused fire. If a fire were to begin, air
quality may diminish in the surrounding area.

likely spread quickly. Outdoor burning is not recommended.

fire weather conditions to develop. Monitor the forecasts for
possible Red Flag Warnings.

ESFBOI

Monsoon moisture will bring a threat of thunderstorms to the region
through Saturday evening for much of the area. High atmospheric
moisture will allow for isolated thunderstorms producing heavy rain
accumulations, leading to an increased threat of flash flooding
especially for the recent wildfire burn scars.

Friday and Saturday have the highest chance for locally heavy rains,
especially near the ID-NV border, and high terrain in southwest
Idaho.

Burn scars have the highest risk for flash flooding. Several burn
scars across the area including the Wapiti burn scar near Grandjean,
ID, the Fox burn scar near Richland, OR, the Tartar burn scar near
Weiser, ID, the Coleman Creek burn scar near Juntura, OR and the Big
Grass Fire  burn scar near Jordan Valley, OR are of particular
concern for flash flooding and debris flows. Please monitor the
latest weather conditions if traveling near these areas.

properties.description:
HLSHFO

This product covers the Hawaiian islands

**HURRICANE WATCH ISSUED FOR THE BIG ISLAND OF HAWAII AS NEWLY
DEVELOPED TROPICAL STORM LALA ADVANCES TOWARD THE HAWAIIAN ISLANDS**

NEW INFORMATION
---------------

* CHANGES TO WATCHES AND WARNINGS:
- A Hurricane Watch has been issued for Big Island East, Big
Island Interior, Big Island North, Big Island South, Big Island
Southeast, Big Island Summits, Kohala, and Kona

* CURRENT WATCHES AND WARNINGS:
- A Hurricane Watch is in effect for Big Island East, Big Island
Interior, Big Island North, Big Island South, Big Island
Southeast, Big Island Summits, Kohala, and Kona

* STORM INFORMATION:
- About 920 miles east-southeast of Honolulu or about 700 miles
east-southeast of Hilo
- 15.2N 145.5W
- Storm Intensity 40 mph
- Movement West or 280 degrees at 10 mph

SITUATION OVERVIEW
------------------

Newly formed Tropical Storm Lala is expected to intensify during the
next few days and bring heavy rainfall, high surf, and potentially
damaging winds to parts of the state this weekend. Some impacts from
Lala could be experienced as early as Friday, mainly over the eastern
end of the island chain, and Lala may move directly over portions of
the state Saturday and Sunday. While the Big Island of Hawaii would
likely be first to experience impacts, do not focus on the exact
forecast track or intensity of Lala at this time, and be prepared for
changes in future forecasts.

Damaging tropical storm force winds may begin as early as Friday night
across parts of the Big Island of Hawaii and could spread westward to
the rest of the state Saturday and Sunday. It is important to note
that the mountainous terrain of the islands can produce localized
areas of highly enhanced and damaging winds, even well away from the
tropical cyclone center.

Flooding rain will be possible as early as Friday night on the Big
Island of Hawaii. The threat of flooding will spread to the rest of
the state on Saturday and Sunday, and heavy rainfall could persist
into Monday for some islands, mainly over the western end of the
island chain. Preliminary storm total rainfall amounts are in the 5 to
10 inch range, with the potential for isolated locations to receive as
much as 20 inches. While the highest rainfall amounts will be focused
over windward areas, leeward areas will also have a significant flood
risk.

Large swells generated by Lala will build late Friday and produce
dangerous surf along exposed east and southeast shores, especially on
the Big Island of Hawaii and Maui. Very large and extremely rough seas
are expected to rapidly increase Saturday and Sunday on exposed
southeast and east shores and may produce damaging surf, significant
beach erosion, and overwash across vulnerable coastal infrastructure.


POTENTIAL IMPACTS
-----------------

* WIND:
Prepare for dangerous wind having possible significant impacts across
the Big Island of Hawaii. Potential impacts in this area include:
- Some damage to roofing and siding materials, along with damage
to porches, awnings, carports, and sheds. A few buildings
experiencing window, door, and garage door failures. Mobile
homes damaged, especially if unanchored. Unsecured lightweight
objects become dangerous projectiles.
- Several large trees snapped or uprooted, but with greater
numbers in places where trees are shallow rooted. Several
fences and roadway signs blown over.
- Some roads impassable from large debris, and more within urban
or heavily wooded places. A few bridges, causeways, and access
routes impassable.
- Scattered power and communications outages, but more prevalent
in areas with above ground lines.

Also, prepare for hazardous wind having possible limited impacts
elsewhere in the state of Hawaii.

* SURGE:
Prepare for locally hazardous surge having possible limited impacts
across portions of the Big Island of Hawaii. Potential impacts in this area
include:
- Localized inundation with storm surge flooding mainly along
immediate shorelines and in low-lying spots, or in areas
farther inland near where higher surge waters move ashore.
- Sections of near-shore roads and parking lots become overspread
with surge water. Driving conditions dangerous in places where
surge water covers the road.
- Moderate beach erosion. Heavy surf also breaching dunes, mainly
in usually vulnerable locations. Strong rip currents.
- Minor to locally moderate damage to marinas, docks, boardwalks,
and piers. A few small craft broken away from moorings.

Elsewhere across the Hawaiian islands, little to no impact is
anticipated.

* FLOODING RAIN:
Prepare for life-threatening rainfall flooding having possible
devastating impacts across the Big Island of Hawaii. Potential
impacts include:
- Extreme rainfall flooding may prompt numerous evacuations and
rescues.
- Rivers and tributaries may overwhelmingly overflow their banks
in many places with deep moving water. Small streams, creeks,
canals, arroyos, and ditches may become raging rivers. In
mountain areas, deadly runoff may rage down valleys while
increasing susceptibility to rockslides and mudslides. Flood
control systems and barriers may become stressed.
- Flood waters can enter numerous structures within multiple
communities, some structures becoming uninhabitable or washed
away. Numerous places where flood waters may cover escape
routes. Streets and parking lots become rivers of raging water
with underpasses submerged. Driving conditions become very
dangerous. Numerous road and bridge closures with some weakened
or washed out.

Prepare for life-threatening rainfall flooding having possible
limited to extensive impacts across the remainder of the state of
Hawaii.

* TORNADOES:
Prepare for a tornado event having possible limited impacts across
the Big Island of Hawaii. Potential impacts include:
- The occurrence of isolated tornadoes can hinder the execution
of emergency plans during tropical events.
- A few places may experience tornado damage, along with power
and communications disruptions.
- Locations could realize roofs peeled off buildings, chimneys
toppled, mobile homes pushed off foundations or overturned,
large tree tops and branches snapped off, shallow-rooted trees
knocked over, moving vehicles blown off roads, and small boats
pulled from moorings.

PRECAUTIONARY/PREPAREDNESS ACTIONS
----------------------------------

* EVACUATIONS:
Listen to local officials for recommended preparedness actions,
including possible evacuations. If ordered to evacuate, do so
immediately.


* OTHER PREPAREDNESS INFORMATION:
Now is the time to check your emergency plan and emergency supplies
kit and take necessary actions to protect your family and secure your
home or business.

When making safety and preparedness decisions, do not focus on the
exact forecast track since hazards such as flooding rain, damaging
wind gusts, storm surge, and tornadoes extend well away from the

properties.description:
ESFHFO

The latest forecast for Potential Tropical Cyclone One-C takes the
system over the state as a strong tropical storm. While One-C is
expected to move steadily west-northwest as it passes through the
island chain, abundant moisture drawn into the circulation will bring
the potential for very heavy rainfall and flash flooding from late
Friday into the weekend across the state.

While the details on the timing and rainfall amounts will highly
depend on the eventual track of the tropical cyclone, we could see
widespread rainfall of 5 to 10 inches. Locally higher amounts will be
possible, especially over the windward areas of Maui and the Big
Island.

Keep up to date with the latest forecast information online at
weather.gov/hawaii, through local media, social media, or NOAA
Weather Radio broadcasts.

An updated outlook will be issued by 5 PM HST Thursday unless
superseded by a Flood Watch.

properties.description:
The Washington State Department of Ecology, Benton Clean Air Agency,
and the Yakima Regional Clean Air Agency have issued an Air Quality
Alert until further notice.

An Air Quality Alert has bee issued for Benton, Columbia, Franklin,
Kittitas, Walla Walla, and Yakima Counties until further notice due
to expected wildfire smoke from regional fires. North to northeast
winds will push smoke into the Columbia Basin beginning Wednesday
afternoon. Particulate matter (PM2.5) levels may reach Unhealthy for
Sensitive Groups or worse. While occasional clearing and intermittent
good air quality is possible during periods of stronger winds, smoke
production continues to be significant from regional fires. Be sure
to check air monitors in your area before outdoor activities. When
air quality is Unhealthy, everyone should reduce exposure. Limit time
outside, avoid strenuous outdoor activity, and follow tips for
cleaner indoor air.


Information from the Washington Department of Ecology web site is
available at http://www.ecy.wa.gov/air.html or call 360-407-6000.
Information from the Yakima Regional Clean Air Agency web site is
available at http://www.yakimacleanair.org or call 509-834-2050.

available at http://www.bentoncleanair.org or call 509-783-1304.
